h1.en: Does a copper peptide serum reduce wrinkles?

byline.en: Appraised by the Skingenetix research team. Medically reviewed by Dr Esther Bodde, Cosmetic & Medical Physician. Last reviewed 24 September 2026.

verdict.en: **Our verdict:** this is the strongest controlled human trial we have for copper peptide, and it is why GHK-Cu is in our range. But the base it was measured against lacked the nano-carrier as well as the peptide, and the paper never states a concentration — so the result belongs to the serum that was tested, not to ours.

v.en: Randomised, double-blind, split-face, run at Dermatest GmbH, an independent cosmetic research institute.
40 women aged 40 to 65. Results are reported for the 39 who completed.
A serum containing GHK-Cu held in a lipid nano-carrier, twice a day, to the right side of the face.
Group 1 (19 women): Strivectin SD Advanced Concentrate, which contains Matrixyl 3000, on the left side. Group 2 (20 women): the plain serum vehicle — no GHK-Cu and no nano-carrier — on the left side.
8 weeks, with measurements at 4 and 8 weeks.
PRIMOS 3D skin imaging of a single large wrinkle near the corner of the eye, over a 30 × 40 mm area.
Never stated. The paper does not report how much GHK-Cu the serum contained.
Funded by Snowberry New Zealand Ltd, which makes the serum, with a Callaghan Innovation grant. The statistical analysis was done independently at the University of Auckland.
A− — randomised and blinded, but small, maker-funded, and published in a journal with weaker peer review.

intro.en: Both sides of every face improved over the eight weeks. The side treated with the GHK-Cu serum improved more, and the gap widened between weeks 4 and 8.

title.en: Change from the start, after 8 weeks

subtitle.en: Group 2 only (20 women): the GHK-Cu serum on the right side of the face, the plain serum vehicle on the left. PRIMOS 3D imaging of one wrinkle near the eye.

label.en: Control serum: no GHK-Cu, no nano-carrier

caption.en: Both sides improved. Against the plain serum vehicle the GHK-Cu side fell further — volume −24.1% against −15.0%, depth −20.3% against −15.3% — which the paper reports as a 55.8% greater reduction in volume (p < 0.0001) and 32.8% in depth (p = 0.0123). The vehicle carried neither the peptide nor the nano-carrier, so the gap covers both (Badenhorst et al., 2016).

alt.en: Laboratory imagery of a collagen network, illustrating the fibroblast arm of the study

body.en: Forty women applied a GHK-Cu serum to the right side of the face twice a day for eight weeks. On the left side, half of them used a product containing Matrixyl 3000 and half used the plain serum base. Neither the women nor the investigators knew which product was which.
A separate arm of the same paper grew human skin cells with GHK-Cu and measured collagen and elastin production, which is where the paper’s laboratory findings come from.

heading.en: What this study does not show

items.en: It does not isolate the copper peptide. The control serum contained neither GHK-Cu nor the lipid nano-carrier that delivered it. The 55.8% therefore covers the peptide and its delivery system together. The authors describe the trial as the first to test GHK-Cu formulated into a nano-carrier.
Our products do not use that nano-carrier. This figure belongs to the serum that was tested, not to ours.
The concentration is never given. Without it, the result cannot be matched to the 2% GHK-Cu we state on our own products.

The sides were not randomised. Every participant received the GHK-Cu serum on the right and the comparator on the left, so any left-right difference in sun exposure or sleeping position sits inside the result.
Against the Matrixyl 3000 product, wrinkle depth was not significant (p = 0.0577). Only the volume difference reached significance there (p = 0.0044).
It is one small trial. 39 people, one site, funded by the maker of the serum, in a journal whose peer review is weaker than the major dermatology titles.

heading.en: What it means for our products

body.en: This is the strongest controlled human trial we have for copper peptide, and it is why GHK-Cu appears in our range at all. But the serum it tested is not ours: it used a lipid nano-carrier and never disclosed its concentration.

So we cite it as evidence for the ingredient, not as a result our products have reproduced. Our own [copper peptide serum](https://www.skingenetix.com/products/copper-peptide-ghk-cu-renewal-serum), day gel-cream and night cream each state 2% GHK-Cu on the pack, which this trial cannot confirm or contradict. The rest of the evidence for the ingredient is set out on the [copper peptide research hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/copper-peptide-research).

answer.en: The Badenhorst 2016 trial is a randomised, double-blind, split-face study of a copper peptide (GHK-Cu) serum in 40 women aged 40 to 65. Over 8 weeks, wrinkle volume on the treated side fell 24.1%, against 15.0% on the plain serum base — a 55.8% greater reduction, measured by 3D imaging.

heading.en: What copper peptide is, and where this trial sits

body.en: Copper peptide, or GHK-Cu, is a chain of three amino acids — glycine, histidine and lysine — bound to a copper ion. It occurs naturally in human blood, where it was first isolated in 1973, and its level falls with age: from about 200 ng/mL at 20 to roughly 80 ng/mL by 60. In skincare it is used to support the look of firmer, smoother skin.

In laboratory work it raises the collagen, elastin and glycosaminoglycans that skin cells produce, and a review by the scientist who first isolated GHK sets out that role in detail ([Pickart et al., 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26236730/)). Evidence in actual skin is thinner: a 2026 systematic review in *Aesthetic Surgery Journal* found GHK-Cu significantly reduced wrinkle volume and depth against controls, but drew on only **two** controlled trials among twenty studies, and said its findings were limited by methodological variability ([Mokhtar et al., 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42619529/)).

This page appraises the stronger of those two trials. It is the reason GHK-Cu is in our range, and it is also the reason we do not claim more than an ingredient-level result. The full picture — every study we rely on, graded — is on the [copper peptide evidence hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/copper-peptide-research), which sits alongside our other [ingredient research](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/the-science).

questions.en: Does this trial prove the ingredient works?
What concentration did the study use?
Do Skingenetix products reproduce this result?

answers.en: It shows that a GHK-Cu serum outperformed a plain serum base on one wrinkle, measured by 3D imaging, in 39 women over 8 weeks. Against a commercial Matrixyl 3000 product it reduced wrinkle volume 31.6% more (p = 0.0044), though the difference in depth was **not statistically significant** (p = 0.0577). It is one small trial, funded by the serum's maker, and the base it beat also lacked the nano-carrier — so it is not proof that copper peptide alone did the work ([Badenhorst et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.4172/2329-8847.1000166)). The other trials we rely on are listed on the [evidence hub](https://www.skingenetix.com/pages/copper-peptide-research).

The paper never states one. That is why no claim on this site says a result was “clinically proven at 2%” — the trial cannot support a concentration claim, and our own products state 2% GHK-Cu on the pack independently of it.

Partly. It was run at Dermatest GmbH, an independent cosmetic research institute, and the statistics were done at the University of Auckland. But it was funded by Snowberry New Zealand Ltd, which makes the serum that was tested, and it was published in a journal whose peer review is weaker than the major dermatology titles. We grade it A− for those reasons.

No, and we do not claim they do. The serum tested here used a lipid nano-carrier that our formulas do not, and its concentration was never disclosed. We cite this trial as evidence for the ingredient, not as a result our products have repeated.
